title: Dengue: assessment and fluid management
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Classify as dengue without warning signs, with warning signs, or severe dengue. Give paracetamol and oral fluids, never NSAIDs. Use haematocrit-guided isotonic crystalloid boluses with stepwise tapering for warning signs and shock, stop IV fluids by 24 to 48 hours, and do not transfuse platelets prophylactically.

sections.title: Recognise and test
items: Phases: febrile (2 to 7 days), critical (plasma leak around defervescence, usually 24 to 48 hours), recovery (2 to 3 days, reabsorption and risk of fluid overload).

Warning signs: persistent vomiting, abdominal pain or tenderness, lethargy or restlessness, mucosal bleeding, syncope or giddiness, clinical fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion), liver enlarged more than 2 cm, rising haematocrit with rapidly falling platelets.
Severe dengue: shock or fluid accumulation with respiratory distress from plasma leak, severe bleeding, AST or ALT 1000 U/L or more, impaired consciousness, or other severe organ involvement.

High risk (admit or observe closely): infants and young children, age over 65, pregnancy, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, heart, kidney or liver disease, haemoglobinopathy or G6PD deficiency, peptic ulcer, long-term steroids or NSAIDs.
Tests: NS1 antigen (ELISA) from day 1 to 5; IgM ELISA after day 5. CBC with haematocrit and platelets for all with warning signs or fever beyond 3 days. Check postural BP and pulse pressure.
Early shock is compensated: tachycardia, capillary refill over 2 seconds, cold extremities, narrow pulse pressure (below 20 mmHg) with normal systolic BP. Hypotension is a late sign.

sections.title: No warning signs (Group A): outpatient
items: Oral fluids (ORS, coconut water, soups); avoid carbonated drinks. Rest. Watch infants for over-hydration.
Paracetamol 10 to 15 mg/kg per dose, no more often than every 6 hours (adult maximum 4 g/day). Tepid sponging.
No aspirin, NSAIDs, steroids or intramuscular injections (WHO 2025 strongly recommends against NSAIDs in acute arboviral disease).
Daily review with CBC and haematocrit, especially from day 3 to defervescence. Teach warning signs and return immediately if any appear.

sections.title: Warning signs without shock (Group B)
items: Admit. Take a baseline haematocrit before fluids if available, but do not delay hydration for it. Encourage oral fluids if tolerated.

If oral intake is poor, haematocrit is rising or warning signs are present: isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline or Ringer lactate) 7 to 10 mL/kg over 1 hour in adults, 5 to 10 mL/kg over 1 hour in children. Use ideal body weight in obesity.

If improving (pulse, BP, pulse pressure, capillary refill, urine output, falling haematocrit): taper to 5 to 7 mL/kg/h for 2 to 4 hours, then 3 to 5 mL/kg/h for 2 to 4 hours, then 2 to 4 mL/kg/h, and stop at 24 to 48 hours.
Not improving and haematocrit still high (above 45%): second crystalloid bolus 10 mL/kg over 1 hour; if still no improvement manage as Group C.
Not improving and haematocrit falling (below 45%): suspect bleeding, check Hb, transfuse whole blood 10 mL/kg or packed red cells 5 mL/kg.
Aim for urine output about 0.5 mL/kg/h (ideal body weight).

sections.title: Severe dengue with shock (Group C)
items: Compensated shock: isotonic crystalloid 10 to 20 mL/kg over 1 hour. If improving, reduce to 7 to 10 mL/kg/h for 1 to 2 hours, 5 to 7 mL/kg/h for 1 to 2 hours, 3 to 5 mL/kg/h for 2 to 4 hours, 2 to 3 mL/kg/h, continuing for up to 24 to 48 hours.
Hypotensive (decompensated) shock: 20 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes (adults up to 500 mL per bolus). If improving, 10 mL/kg/h for 1 hour, then taper as above.
Shock persists with haematocrit still high (above 45%): repeat bolus 10 to 20 mL/kg over 15 to 30 minutes; up to three rapid boluses. Then taper to 7 to 10 mL/kg/h once improving.
Shock persists with haematocrit falling (below 40% in children and women, below 45% in men) or below baseline: occult bleeding; cross-match and transfuse whole blood 10 mL/kg or packed cells 5 mL/kg.
Refractory shock: ICU, vasopressors or inotropes, echo for myocardial dysfunction, and look for acidosis, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hidden haemorrhage and bacterial sepsis.
NCVBDC allows colloid (for example dextran 40) for massive leak not responding to maximum crystalloid; WHO 2025 suggests crystalloids rather than colloids.

sections.title: Monitoring and when to stop fluids
items: Vital signs and peripheral perfusion every 2 to 4 hours without shock, every 1 to 2 hours in shock, and every 5 to 30 minutes during resuscitation.
Haematocrit before and after each bolus (not during), then every 4 to 6 hours in stable patients. A 10% rise above baseline is an early sign of plasma leak.
Hourly urine output in shock (catheterise); maintain a fluid balance chart. Glucose, electrolytes, calcium, renal and liver function, coagulation, lactate as indicated.

Stop or reduce IV fluids when BP, pulse and perfusion are normal, haematocrit falls with good pulse volume, afebrile 24 to 48 hours without antipyretics, abdominal symptoms settle and urine output improves. IV fluids beyond 48 hours of the critical phase risk pulmonary oedema.

sections.title: Bleeding, platelets and fluid overload
items: Platelet count does not predict bleeding. No prophylactic platelet transfusion (WHO 2025: not for counts below 50,000/mm3 without active bleeding).
NCVBDC: transfuse platelets for active bleeding; prophylactic transfusion may be considered only below 10,000/mm3 (for example in adults with hypertension) or before emergency surgery.
Severe bleeding: identify and control the source (nasal packing, endoscopy); replace with fresh whole blood 10 mL/kg or packed cells 5 mL/kg aliquots.

Fluid overload (puffy eyelids, tense ascites, rising respiratory rate, crackles): stop hypotonic fluids, check acidosis, bleeding, calcium and glucose; if haemodynamically stable give furosemide 1 mg/kg IV and monitor response.
No role for corticosteroids or immunoglobulin (WHO 2025).

sections.title: Pregnancy, infants and comorbidities
items: Pregnancy: high risk of shock, bleeding and fluid overload; baseline haematocrit is lower, so interpret rises carefully. Involve obstetrics; near term, monitor the neonate for shock mimicking sepsis.

Infants: use isotonic crystalloid throughout the critical period; 0.45% saline may be used in infants under 6 months. Calculate maintenance by Holliday-Segar (100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 mL/kg/day for the next 10 kg, 20 mL/kg/day thereafter).
Hypertensive patients may be hypotensive at 'normal' BP readings; compare with their baseline.
Encephalopathy: look for hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hepatic failure or intracranial bleed; keep IV fluid at or below 80% of maintenance, head up 30 degrees.

sections.title: Admission and discharge
items: Admit all with warning signs, severe dengue, or high-risk features with poor oral intake. Severe dengue needs a hospital with blood transfusion facilities; decompensated shock needs ICU.
Group B patients who recover rapidly and are not in the critical phase may go home after 12 to 24 hours with daily review.

Discharge when afebrile for at least 24 hours without antipyretics, appetite returns, haematocrit stable at baseline, no respiratory distress from effusions or ascites, at least 2 to 3 days after recovery from shock, and platelet count above 50,000/mm3.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating the platelet count instead of the haematocrit and perfusion.
Continuing large IV volumes into the recovery phase, causing pulmonary oedema.
Missing concealed bleeding when shock persists with a falling haematocrit.
Giving NSAIDs, aspirin or IM injections for fever and body ache.
Discharging at defervescence, which is exactly when the critical phase begins.

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 10 to 15 mg/kg orally per dose, no more often than 6-hourly; adults 500 mg to 1 g per dose, maximum 4 g/day
drugs.notes: Only antipyretic to use. Avoid aspirin and all NSAIDs.

drugs.name: Isotonic crystalloid (0.9% saline or Ringer lactate)
drugs.dose: Warning signs: 7 to 10 mL/kg over 1 hour (children 5 to 10 mL/kg). Compensated shock: 10 to 20 mL/kg over 1 hour. Hypotensive shock: 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes
drugs.notes: Taper stepwise by haematocrit and clinical response; stop by 24 to 48 hours. Use ideal body weight in obesity.

drugs.name: Whole blood or packed red cells
drugs.dose: Whole blood 10 mL/kg or packed red cells 5 mL/kg per aliquot
drugs.notes: Shock with falling haematocrit or overt severe bleeding.

drugs.name: Platelet concentrate
drugs.dose: Only for active bleeding; consider prophylaxis only below 10,000/mm3 or before emergency surgery
drugs.notes: Prophylactic transfusion does not prevent bleeding and causes adverse events.

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.notes: Fluid overload once haemodynamically stable; monitor vital signs every 15 minutes for 1 hour afterwards.
